title: How to Honor Your Body as a Christian
excerpt: The body is not a cage the soul is trapped in, and it is not the whole of who you are. It is a good gift, made and bought and bound for resurrection.
body:
There is an old lie that keeps coming back wearing new clothes. It says the body is a shell, a piece of equipment the real you rides around in, and that the spiritual life is mostly about escaping it. The church fought this lie in its first centuries and thought it had won. We rebuilt it twice. Once in the people who treat the body as disposable, who run it into the ground and call the ruin commitment. Once in the people who treat the body as the whole self, an endless project at the mirror that is never finished and never enough. Both are forms of contempt. Neither is Christian.

I have lived in both ditches. I have ignored my body until it sent a bill I could not argue with, and I have stood in front of the mirror running an audit nobody assigned me. The way out of both is the same, and it is not a technique. It is a doctrine, held until it changes how you live in your own skin.

## You do not have a body, you are one

Genesis says God formed the man from dust and breathed into him, and the man became a living being. Not received a body. Became one. And God looked at the whole material world he had made, dust and breath and flesh, and called it very good. Embodiment is not the problem the gospel comes to solve. It is the good gift that sin has bent.

Then the part that ends the argument for good. The Word became flesh. God did not redeem the world from a safe distance. He took on a body, got hungry, slept in a boat through a storm because he was tired, ate fish after the resurrection to prove the body was real. The risen Christ still has a body. Whatever your relationship with your own body has been, contempt is no longer available to you as a Christian option. God wore one.

## Bought, not your own

Paul tells the Corinthians that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and we have printed that on gym walls as if he meant mileage and protein. Read it in its place. Paul is writing to people using their bodies for sexual sin, and his point is ownership. You were bought with a price, so glorify God in your body. It does not say make the temple impressive. It says remember whose it is.

This cuts both ways, which is the part we miss. If your body is not your own, then neglect is a kind of theft, spending down something that belongs to God. But idolatry is theft too, taking what belongs to God and bowing to it. The body is a steward's trust, not a god to serve and not a junk car to drive into the ground.

## Honor is not optimization

Here is where it gets practical and where most of us go wrong. We hear honor your body and immediately reach for a plan, a regimen, a number to hit. But honor in Scripture is closer to reverence than to improvement. You honor the body the way you honor a gift, by receiving it, using it well, and not despising it.

That means sleeping enough to admit you are a creature. It means eating with thanks instead of guilt. It means moving in a way that comes from gratitude for a working body rather than punishment of a failing one. And it means, when the body weakens, which it will, refusing the lie that a weak body is a worthless one. The man dying of cancer honors his body no less than the athlete. He honors it by receiving what is left of it from God's hand without bitterness.

One plain word. If your relationship with your body has become frightening or compulsive, if eating or the mirror or exercise has tangled itself up with punishment, that is not a willpower failure and not a sin to pray away alone. It is a medical and psychological matter. See a doctor. See a counselor. Needing help is not the opposite of faith. It is often what faith looks like.

## The end of the story is a body

The Bible does not close with souls floating free of their bodies in some misty heaven. It closes with resurrection, bodies raised on a renewed earth. Whatever your body becomes, it is not headed for the trash. It is headed, by the mercy of God, for glory. That changes how you carry it now. You are not maintaining a temporary vehicle. You are caring for something God intends to keep.

## This week

Pick one ordinary bodily thing you usually do with contempt, eating fast and distracted, staying up past the point of sense, looking at yourself with that critical eye, and do it once this week with honor instead. Eat one meal slowly and give thanks for it. Go to bed on time as an act of trust. Catch yourself in the mirror and say, out loud if you can, that this body is a gift God made and intends to raise. You will feel how strange it is to bless what you are used to managing or despising. Stay with the strangeness. It is the doctrine working its way down into your hands.

title: How to Build Rhythms of Work and Rest
excerpt: We are the first society with no shared rhythm of rest, no hour when it is collectively bedtime and no day when it is collectively Sabbath. Nobody is handing the pattern back. It has to be rebuilt.
body:
There used to be a shape to time, and most of us have never lived inside it. The workday ended. Shops closed on Sunday. The church bell, and before that the sun, told a whole town when to work and when to stop. You did not have to be disciplined to rest, because rest was built into the world around you, and the structure carried you.

That structure is gone. The phone in your pocket is a factory whistle that never stops blowing. There is no hour now when it is collectively bedtime, no day when it is collectively Sabbath, no shared signal that says the work can wait until morning. We are the first society in human history with no agreed rhythm of rest at all. We did not vote for this, and nobody is going to vote it back. The pattern will have to be rebuilt by hand, household by household, on purpose, or it will not exist.

## Rhythm is older than the law

Before there was a single commandment, there was a rhythm. God worked for six days and rested on the seventh, and Genesis says the rest was built into the structure of time before anyone had sinned. The Sabbath is not a rule bolted onto a tired creation as damage control. It is part of how the world was made, a stop woven into the fabric of time the way breathing is woven into a body.

This matters because it means rest is not a reward you earn by working hard enough. It is the shape of the week as God designed it. Six and one. Work that has an end. You are not built to run flat out forever, and the proof is not your exhaustion, though that is real. The proof is the seventh day, sitting there in the first chapter of the Bible, before any of us showed up.

## The two failures

Most of us fail at this in one of two directions, and you probably know which is yours.

The first is the workaholic's failure, no real off. The work bleeds into the evening, the weekend, the vacation, the bed. There is no hour you are truly unreachable, no day the laptop stays closed. You tell yourself it is just this season, but the seasons have a way of lasting a decade. Underneath it is usually a quiet conviction that the world cannot run without you, which is not humility about your importance but pride about it.

The second is the opposite and just as real, no rhythm at all, work and leisure smeared together into one gray undifferentiated mush. You are never fully working and never fully resting. The phone is always half-out, so the leisure is never restful and the work is never finished. This is the more common failure now, and it is worse than the first, because at least the workaholic knows he is working.

## Build the boundary, not the feeling

The mistake is to wait until you feel rested before you rest, or to wait until the work is done before you stop. The work is never done. That is the nature of the work. So you do not stop because you finished. You stop because the time came, the same way you do not eat dinner only when the day is complete.

Start with one hard edge. Pick a time in the evening when work ends, and let it end there, screen closed, notifications off, the unfinished thing left unfinished until morning. The first nights will feel like negligence. They are not. They are trust. Psalm 127 calls the bread of anxious late-night toil vanity, because God gives sleep to his beloved. The work you leave undone goes into better hands than yours overnight.

Then build the larger stop, a weekly stretch of real rest. It does not have to be a perfect Sabbath to start. A half day. No work, no buying, a shared table, something that feels like delight rather than duty. The point is a stop your soul can lean against, a day that announces, by its mere existence, that you are not a slave and the world is not yours to hold up.

## Rest is a confession

In Deuteronomy the Sabbath command is grounded in liberation. You were slaves in Egypt, and slaves never get a day off. So your weekly rest is a declaration that Pharaoh is not your master anymore. Every time you stop, you are confessing that your worth is not your output, that the God who ran the world while you slept will run it while you rest, and that you are a beloved creature and not a machine. The rhythm preaches this to you when you cannot preach it to yourself.

## This week

Draw one line and one stop. Pick an hour this week when work ends, and actually end it there, screen closed, three nights running. Then block one half day, even four hours, with no work and no buying in it, and put one thing in that window that is pure delight. Do not aim to fix your whole broken relationship with time by Sunday. Aim to put one edge back into a week that has lost all of them, and to feel, even briefly, what it is like to stop because the time came and not because the work ran out.

title: How to Sleep Like a Creature Who Trusts God
excerpt: Sleep is not lost productivity. It is a nightly act of trust, hours of unconsciousness in which you admit that God runs the world and you do not.
body:
The most common way a day ends now is with a glowing rectangle six inches from a face, trading the sleep we need for one more scroll, one more episode, one more refresh. I am not describing you from across the room. I have looked up from the phone at one in the morning more times than I want to admit, knowing exactly what the next day would cost, and done the same thing the next night. Sleep is the clearest evidence of how we treat the body, and most of us treat it like an enemy to be outlasted.

We have built a whole culture of contempt around it. We boast about running on five hours. We treat the need for sleep as a weakness to be conquered by the strong and tolerated by the weak. And the science keeps confirming, in study after study, what the boast culture refuses to hear, that chronic sleep loss degrades memory, mood, immunity, and judgment, and that no amount of grit exempts anyone. But the science can only tell you that sleep works. It cannot tell you what sleep is for. For that you have to go back further.

## Sleep is a theology

Psalm 127 says it is vain to rise early and stay up late eating the bread of anxious toil, for God gives sleep to his beloved. Sit with that. Every night, you lose consciousness for a third of your life. You stop working, stop watching, stop holding anything up. The world goes on without your supervision, and in the morning it is still there. Sleep is a nightly rehearsal of a truth your waking self keeps forgetting, that you are not the one holding the world together.

The person who cannot sleep is often the person who cannot stop being God for long enough to rest. The mind races through tomorrow because some part of you believes that if you stop attending to it all, it will fall apart. Sleep is the body's nightly contradiction of that belief. You lie down, you let go, and the God who neither slumbers nor sleeps keeps the watch you cannot keep.

## The body cannot be tricked

Gratitude for this truth does not exempt you from the design. God gives sleep to his beloved, but he gives it through a body that has rules, and the rules are not optional just because you love Jesus. A creature that floods itself with light until midnight and pours caffeine on its exhaustion is fighting its own design, and the design wins.

So the practice is humble and physical. Give the body the conditions it needs and then trust it to do its work. A consistent time to lie down, near the same hour each night, so the body knows when to release. Darkness, because the body reads light as a command to stay awake. And the hardest one, distance from the screen, because the phone is engineered to keep you up and it is winning against your willpower every single night.

## Give your phone a bedtime before your own

Here is the single most practical thing in this whole piece. Give your phone a bedtime an hour before yours, and charge it somewhere outside the bedroom. Not on the nightstand. In another room. The reason is simple and a little humbling. You will not out-discipline a device designed by thousands of people to hold your attention. The only winning move is to put it where your hand cannot reach it half-asleep.

The hour between the phone going to bed and you going to bed is not wasted time. It is the runway the body needs to come down. Read something on paper. Pray. Talk to your spouse. Let the day actually end instead of being severed mid-scroll.

## When sleep will not come

Sometimes the body does everything right and sleep still will not come, and I want to be honest that no devotional tip fixes that. Chronic insomnia, sleep apnea, the wakefulness that comes with grief or depression or trauma, these are real and some of them need a doctor. If you have done the ordinary things and sleep still will not come, that is not a faith failure to pray harder against. Go get help. The God who gives sleep to his beloved often gives it through a physician.

And on the nights you simply lie awake, let even that become a kind of trust. The psalmist speaks of remembering God on his bed and meditating in the watches of the night. A wakeful hour does not have to be a wasted one. It can be an hour given back to the One who is awake with you.

## This week

Do two small things. Pick a bedtime and keep it three nights this week, not a perfect one, a real one you can actually meet. And give your phone a bedtime an hour before your own, charging it in another room. When you lie down, before sleep takes you, say one true sentence to God, something like, the work is unfinished and I am leaving it with you. You are not optimizing tomorrow. You are practicing, in the dark, the trust that the world holds together without your hands on it, because it always has.

title: How to Eat and Feast Without Guilt or Excess
excerpt: Almost none of us simply eat. We manage, we reward, we punish, we apologize. The table was meant to be a place of gratitude and communion before it was ever a matter of nutrition.
body:
Watch how people eat and you will see what they believe about themselves. For some, food is comfort, the thing the hand reaches for when the day has emptied them out. For some it is control, the one corner of a chaotic life that will still obey. For some it is guilt, every meal arriving with a verdict attached, a running tally of what has been earned and what must now be repaid. Almost none of us simply eat. We manage, we reward, we punish, we apologize. The plain act of receiving food with thanks has become rare.

The two failures here mirror each other. There is excess, the appetite that has become its own master, that eats past fullness and past gratitude into numbness. And there is its respectable twin, the obsessive control that treats every bite as a moral event, that has turned the table into a courtroom. The church has tended to thunder against the first and quietly admire the second, calling it discipline. Scripture is suspicious of both.

## A word that has to come first

Before anything else. If eating has become frightening, or compulsive, or tangled up with punishment, if you skip meals out of fear or eat in secret out of shame or cannot sit at a table without a war going on inside you, that is not a willpower problem and not a faith problem to be prayed away alone. It is a medical and psychological matter, and a serious one. See a doctor. See a counselor. God is not ashamed of you for needing help, and getting it is an act of faith, not a failure of it. Nothing else in this piece applies until that is said.

## The table before the label

The modern food environment is engineered to make us eat badly and constantly. We are being discipled by packaging and marketing far more than by any wisdom, taught to think of eating as fuel and nutrients and macros, a delivery system for the body rather than a human practice. Recovering the meal as a meal is most of the battle.

Scripture treats food as gift before it is ever nutrition. Everything God created is good, Paul writes to Timothy, and is to be received with thanksgiving. That single word reframes the whole thing. Eating is meant to be an act of gratitude and communion, a daily return to the God who made wheat and fish and oil and the tongue that tastes them. The center of eating is not the label. It is the table, and the thanks said over it.

## Jesus came eating

It is worth saying loudly, especially to the guilt-bound, that Jesus came eating and drinking, and his enemies called him a glutton and a drunkard for it. He was forever at someone's table. He made wine at a wedding when the wine ran out. His first miracle was not feeding a fast. It was keeping a feast going. The kingdom of God, in his own image for it, is a banquet.

So a Christianity of perpetual anxious restriction slanders the Giver. If every meal is a guilty negotiation, something has gone wrong with your theology before anything has gone wrong with your diet. Food is a gift, and the right response to a gift is thanks, not apology. You are allowed to enjoy your dinner. You are allowed to feast.

## And freedom that can still say no

But hear the other side, because grace is not the same as appetite. The same Paul who calls all food good also says he will not be mastered by anything. Freedom that never declines anything has quietly become appetite with a verse attached. The feast is good precisely because it is a feast and not the daily condition, an arrival that means something because there are ordinary days around it.

The practice, then, is not a rule about quantities. It is the slow recovery of eating as gift, which heals both ditches at once. The glutton learns that more is not the way to satisfaction, because the joy was never in the volume. The anxious controller learns that food is allowed, that thanks can replace the audit. Both are being led to the same plain table, where you receive what is given, eat it with gratitude, and stop without ceremony when you have had enough.

## Feasting is a discipline too

We think of discipline as restraint, but feasting takes its own discipline, the discipline of actually being present and grateful instead of distracted and numb. Eating one meal slowly, with thanks, no screen in sight, tasting the food and noticing that it was given, is harder than skipping a meal for many of us. It requires you to be in your body, at a table, receiving. That is a spiritual act, and most of us have lost the muscle for it.

## This week

Eat one meal slowly this week, with thanks, with no screen anywhere in sight. Taste the food. Name one specific thing on the table you are grateful for, out loud, the bread, the person across from you, the fact that there is enough. And once this week, if your history allows it, let yourself genuinely feast, a real meal with people, enjoyed without the running tally, received as the gift it is. You are not on a program. You are learning, slowly, to do the oldest and simplest thing, to receive your food from God's hand and say thank you.

title: How to Steward Your Health
excerpt: Health is not yours to optimize and it is not yours to neglect. It is a trust, held loosely, cared for as a gift and surrendered when it goes, without idolizing it and without despising it.
body:
There is a way of caring about your health that is really a way of trying to be immortal, an anxious project of postponement, every supplement and screening and regimen a small bid against death. And there is a way of ignoring your health that pretends to be spiritual, as if a body run into the ground were proof of devotion. Most of us drift toward one or the other, and the Christian word for the middle path is stewardship, which is harder than either ditch because it asks you to care without idolizing and to surrender without despising.

A steward is not an owner. A steward takes good care of something that belongs to someone else, and a steward also knows it is not finally his to keep. Hold both halves at once and you have the right posture toward your health. It matters, because the body is the instrument of every other act of love you will ever perform. And it is not ultimate, because the body is headed for the grave and then, by mercy, for resurrection.

## Why the body is worth tending

Start with why this is not vanity. Your body is the only instrument you have for loving anyone. Patience happens in a body, in a kitchen at the end of a long day, choosing a gentle answer on low reserves. Generosity, service, presence, every concrete act of love runs through a body. Let the instrument rust through neglect and you have less of yourself to give. Stewarding your health is not self-absorption. It is keeping the tool sharp for the work of love.

This reframes the ordinary things. Sleep, movement, food, the boring fundamentals of bodily care are not a side project running alongside the spiritual life. They are part of it, the material out of which a life of service is actually built. A discipleship that never touches your calendar, your kitchen, and your bed is theory.

## Use the doctors

Let me say something the spiritualizers need to hear. Going to the doctor is an act of stewardship, not a failure of faith. The same God who heals also made the bodies of physicians and the minds that learned medicine, and Scripture has no quarrel with using them. Luke, who wrote a gospel, was a physician. Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach. The faith that refuses ordinary medical care in the name of trusting God is not stronger faith. It is often pride wearing piety's clothes.

So get the screening. Take the medication that keeps you well. See the specialist when something is wrong. Especially the things we are tempted to ignore, the chest pain we explain away, the mole we keep meaning to check, the mental health we treat as a character flaw rather than a condition. Stewardship means not gambling with a trust that is not yours.

## Care without idolatry

Now the other side, because our culture's real religion is health, and the gym has become a rival sanctuary. There is a way of pursuing wellness that has become its own god, an endless anxious campaign for a body that will never be good enough and that death is going to take regardless. The supplements, the tracking, the optimizing, all of it can become a liturgy of self-salvation, a refusal to accept that you are a creature who is going to die.

The tell is anxiety and the mirror. Care offered as gratitude for a working body is stewardship. Care driven by fear of decline, by punishment, by the reflection that is never lean enough or strong enough, is something else, and it should be named gently and brought into the light. Bodily training is of some value, Paul tells Timothy, while godliness is of value in every way. Some value. Real and relative. The man who has made health his ultimate has built his house on something that is, by design, sand.

## Hold it with an open hand

The deepest part of stewarding your health is being ready to lose it. You will. Strength fades, organs fail, the body that served you so long will one day stop. A steward who clutches the trust as if it were his own will be undone when it is taken. A steward who held it with an open hand can watch it go with grief but without terror, because he always knew it was on loan.

Teach us to number our days, the psalmist prays, that we may get a heart of wisdom. The wisest thing about your health is the knowledge that it is temporary, that this body is a gift you are tending for a while and then laying down in trust, in the sure hope that the One who made it intends to raise it.

## This week

Do one neglected thing and drop one anxious thing. Schedule the appointment you have been putting off, the checkup, the screening, the counselor, whatever you have been spiritualizing your way out of. And find one place where your care for your health has curdled into fear or vanity, the obsessive tracking, the punishing measurement, and let it go for the week as an experiment in trust. You are not maintaining a machine and you are not building an idol. You are tending a gift you will one day return, and learning to do it with thanks rather than fear.

title: How to Care for Your Body in Sickness
excerpt: Sickness strips away the lie that you are in control. It is not a punishment to be ashamed of or a problem to be willed away, but a season to be received, with real medical help and a faith that can rest.
body:
Something changes the day you get sick in a way that does not quickly pass. The world that seemed to run on your effort goes on without you. The to-do list waits. The plans dissolve. And you are left in a body that will not do what you tell it, learning a lesson you spent your whole healthy life avoiding, that you were never as in control as you thought. Sickness is one of the great unmaskers. It takes away the illusion of self-sufficiency, and that loss, however bitter, is closer to the truth than the illusion was.

I want to talk about how to be sick as a Christian, because the church often handles this badly, either by treating illness as a faith problem to be conquered or by spiritualizing it into a tidy lesson. It is neither. It is a hard season to be walked through with honesty, and there are better and worse ways to walk it.

## Get the medical help, fully

Let me start where the spiritualizers will not. Use the doctors. Use them fully. Take the treatment, the medication, the surgery, the therapy. The faith that refuses real medical care in the name of trusting God for healing is not stronger faith, and it has gotten people killed. The God who heals works most often through the ordinary means of medicine, through the slow patient labor of physicians and nurses, and there is nothing unspiritual about a hospital. If anything, receiving care well is its own act of humility for people used to being the helper rather than the helped.

So do not pit prayer against treatment. Pray and take the medicine. Ask God for healing and keep the appointment. The two were never enemies. The same God who can heal directly is the one who gave us the knowledge to heal through skill, and using that knowledge honors him.

## Let the body rest without guilt

Many of us cannot be sick without shame. We feel the weight of everything not getting done, the burden we have become to others, the guilt of lying still while the world keeps working. This is the workaholic's last fortress, the inability to rest even when the body has forced the issue.

Sickness is the body insisting on the rest you would not take. Receiving it without guilt is part of the work. You are not lazy because you are ill. You are not failing because you cannot carry what you used to carry. The need to lie still is not a moral failing. It is the design of a creature that has limits, made plain. Let people help you. Let the work wait. The Sabbath you would not give yourself, the body is now giving you, and fighting it only adds shame to suffering.

## Bring God your anger and fear, not a brave face

The church sometimes pressures the sick to perform faith, to be a good witness, to keep smiling and saying the right things. This is cruelty dressed as encouragement. The Psalms are full of sick and suffering people who say exactly how bad it is, who cry out, who ask God how long and even why. That is not a lapse of faith. That is faith being honest.

You do not have to protect God from your fear or your anger about being ill. Bring it to him raw. The God who took on a body and suffered in it is not put off by your suffering or your honest words about it. A faith that can only say the cheerful thing is brittle. A faith that can say, this is terrible and I am afraid and I still trust you, is the durable kind, and it is the kind the Psalms model on nearly every page.

## Receive care as part of the body of Christ

When Paul describes the church as a body, he means that when one part suffers, all suffer with it. Sickness is where that becomes concrete. The meals dropped off, the rides to appointments, the prayers prayed over you when you cannot pray for yourself. For independent people this is the hardest part, learning to receive instead of give.

Receiving care is not weakness, and refusing it is not strength. It is a kind of pride that will not let others love you. Let them. You have spent your life, perhaps, being the one who helps. Sickness is your turn to let the body of Christ be the body of Christ toward you, and that grace is real even when it is hard to accept.

## When healing does not come

Sometimes the healing comes and sometimes it does not, and a faithful word has to hold both. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and it was not, and he was told that grace would be sufficient instead. Not every sickness is healed in this life. The hope of the gospel is not that you will never be sick but that sickness does not get the last word, that this body, even if it fails, is bound for resurrection. We grieve what illness takes, and the grief is real, but we do not grieve as those without hope.

## This week

If you are sick right now, do two things. Make sure you are getting the real medical help you need, not spiritualizing your way around it, and if you are not, make the call this week. And tell God the truth about how it actually is, out loud or written down, the fear and the anger and all of it, without the brave face. Then let one person help you with something, and receive it without apology. You are a creature with limits, in a body that is bound for resurrection, and you are allowed to be sick without shame and held while you are.

title: How to Age With Grace
excerpt: Our culture handles aging by hiding it or fighting it with ever more elaborate programs of postponement. Christians can simply look at it, grieving what it takes without grieving as those who have no hope.
body:
Our whole culture is organized around the refusal to age. We hide the old in facilities and the dying in hospitals, and for those still in the game we sell an endless war against the clock, the creams and procedures and supplements that promise to hold off what is coming. The message underneath all of it is that aging is a defeat, a failure of will or money or vigilance, something to be fought to the last and never accepted. This is a strange way to treat the one thing that happens to everyone who is fortunate enough to live.

Christians can do something the culture cannot. We can simply look at aging, without the panic and without the denial. We can grieve what it takes, honestly, and still refuse the terror, because the body's story does not end at the grave. Aging with grace is not pretending it does not hurt. It is facing it with hope.

## Honor your own decline

There is real loss in aging and it does no good to pretend otherwise. The strength fades. The body that once did what you asked now negotiates. The names come slower, the stairs come harder, the mirror shows someone you do not quite recognize. Faith does not require you to be cheerful about this. The Psalms include the prayer, do not cast me off in the time of old age, do not forsake me when my strength is spent. That is an honest prayer, and God put it in the book.

So grieve what is real. Aging takes things, and the losses deserve to be named, not minimized with a forced smile. But grieve as one who has hope, because the grief is not the whole story. The decline of the body is not the decline of the person. The outer self wastes away, Paul writes, while the inner self is being renewed day by day. The two can run in opposite directions at once, the body weakening while the soul deepens, and that is not denial. That is the actual design.

## There is a glory reserved for the old

Our culture worships youth, and the church has too often gone along, building everything around the young and quietly sidelining the old. Scripture flips it. Gray hair is a crown of glory, Proverbs says, gained in a righteous life. The old were meant to be the keepers of wisdom and memory, the ones who had walked the long road and could tell you what they found.

If you are aging, you have something the young cannot have and cannot fake, the perspective that only decades give. The faithfulness of God across a whole life, seen from the far end. The lessons paid for in failure and grief. This is not consolation for losing your youth. It is a real glory the young do not yet possess. The task of the old is not to mimic the young but to become what only age can make, a person of seasoned wisdom whose presence steadies a room. Do not despise your gray hair. It is a crown.

## Receive help as you once gave it

The hardest turn in aging, for the strong especially, is the move from giver to receiver. There comes a point where you need help with things you once did without thinking, and for a lifelong helper this can feel like a humiliation. It is not. It is a return to the truth you always lived inside but could ignore while you were strong, that you are a dependent creature, held by God and meant to be held by others.

Jesus told Peter that when he was old he would stretch out his hands and another would dress him and carry him where he did not want to go. Even that loss of independence, Jesus framed as a way of glorifying God. To receive care with grace, to let others do for you what you can no longer do for yourself, is not the end of usefulness. It is its own kind of witness, a daily lesson in dependence that the proud and able never get to learn.

## And get the care your body needs

A plain word among the theology. Aging well includes ordinary good medical care, and there is nothing unfaithful about it. Get the screenings, treat the conditions, take the medications that keep you well and present. Pay attention to the body and mind both, because the changes of age, in memory and mood as much as in the joints, often have real help available. Stewardship does not stop because you are old. Caring for an aging body is still caring for a gift.

## The hope that changes everything

The reason a Christian can age without terror is the resurrection. This body will weaken and fail and be buried, and that is not the end of it. We grieve, but not as those without hope, because the same God who made this body intends to raise it, renewed and incorruptible. The old believer is not winding down toward nothing. He is, strange as it sounds, closer to the beginning than the young are, nearer to the morning when the body is raised. That hope does not erase the losses. It puts them in their place.

## This week

If you are aging, do two things. Name one loss honestly, to God or to someone you trust, without rushing to make it okay, because the grief is allowed. And name one thing the years have given you, some wisdom or perspective or steadiness that the young around you do not yet have, and find one young person to give it to this week, a word, a story, an hour of real attention. You are not winding down toward nothing. You are a crown of glory carrying a lifetime of God's faithfulness, headed for a morning when this tired body is raised.

title: How to Live With Chronic Pain and Faith
excerpt: Chronic pain is the suffering the church understands least, because it does not resolve. Faith here is not a cure but a way to keep trusting God inside a body that hurts and will not stop.
body:
Most of what the church says about suffering assumes the suffering will end. There is the trial, then the deliverance, the testimony of how God brought you through. But chronic pain does not work that way. It does not resolve into a tidy story. It is the ache that was there when you woke and will be there when you sleep, the condition you have learned the whole shape of, the thing that does not get better and may never. This is the suffering the church understands least, and the people living inside it often feel most alone, because the usual scripts do not fit.

I write this carefully, knowing I am addressing people who have heard a lot of bad theology about their bodies, who have been told they lack faith, who have been prayed over and pressured and left more wounded than helped. I want to say something truer and gentler than that.

## First, the medical care is not optional

Before any of the theology, this. Chronic pain is a medical reality that needs medical care, and managing it well, with doctors, with appropriate treatment, with whatever genuinely reduces the suffering, is wisdom and stewardship, not weakness or worldliness. The spiritualizing that tells sufferers to pray harder instead of getting real treatment is cruelty. Use the medicine. See the specialists. Take the pain seriously as a body problem, because it is one. Faith does not replace care. It walks alongside it.

And the mental weight that comes with chronic pain, the depression and despair that so often ride along with it, those need real care too. Persistent pain wears the soul down, and there is no shame in needing help for that part. Getting it is faithful, not faithless.

## You do not have to pretend it is fine

The pressure on the chronically ill to perform faith is enormous and damaging. Be a good witness, keep smiling, do not complain. This is not biblical. The Bible is full of people in long suffering who say exactly how bad it is. Job did not bless God quietly through his agony. He cried out, he protested, he demanded an answer, and God did not rebuke the honesty. The Psalms have language for pain that goes on and on, how long, O Lord, will you forget me forever.

So you are allowed to say it hurts. You are allowed to be angry about a body that will not stop hurting. You do not have to protect God from your honesty or perform a serenity you do not feel. A faith that can only manage the cheerful version is brittle and will break under real pain. The durable kind is the kind that can say, this is unbearable and I still will not let go of you. That is not weak faith. That is the strongest faith there is.

## Where is God in the pain

The question underneath chronic pain is always the same. Where is God in this. And the Christian answer is not a explanation but a person. We do not worship a God who watches suffering from a safe distance. We worship one who took on a body and suffered in it, who knew physical agony from the inside, whose risen body still bears the wounds. Whatever else is unclear, this is not. God is not absent from your pain. He has been inside pain like it.

This does not explain why the pain continues, and I will not pretend it does. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be taken away, and the answer was not removal but presence, grace will be sufficient for you, my power is made perfect in weakness. That is a hard word and an honest one. Sometimes the thorn stays. The promise is not that it will go but that God will be sufficient inside it, and that the weakness itself becomes a strange place where his strength shows up.

## Find the smaller mercies

When the pain does not lift, the soul has to learn to live on smaller mercies, and learning to see them is its own discipline. Not the big deliverance, but the hour that was a little easier, the friend who sat with you, the morning light, the meal you could taste. The chronically ill who keep their faith are often the ones who have trained their eyes to find these, not as denial of the pain but as proof that grace has not departed, that even here, in a body that hurts, God still gives good gifts.

This is not toxic positivity. It is the opposite. It looks the pain full in the face, refuses to pretend it is less than it is, and still insists on noticing the mercies that survive alongside it. Both are true at once. The pain is real and the mercy is real, and faith is the refusal to let either one erase the other.

## The hope that does not depend on healing

The deepest comfort for chronic pain is not the promise of a cure in this life, which may not come. It is the resurrection. This body, the one that hurts now, is bound to be raised, made new, free of the pain that has marked it. We grieve what the pain takes, and the grief is real and long, but we do not grieve as those without hope. There is a morning coming for this body. The pain is not forever, even if it is for now, even if it is for the rest of this life. It does not get the last word.

## This week

Do two things, gently. Make sure you are actually getting the medical and mental care your pain needs, and if there is a gap, take one step to close it this week, a call, an appointment, an honest conversation with a doctor. And give yourself permission to tell God the unedited truth, the how-long and the why and the anger, in the words the Psalms already gave you. Then look for one small mercy in the day, just one, and name it. You are not failing at faith because the pain stays. You are carrying a real cross in a real body, held by a God who has been inside pain like yours, toward a morning when this body is raised.

title: How to Unhook From Your Screens
excerpt: The phone is a factory whistle that never stops blowing. Attention is a form of love, and you are giving yours, all day, to a device engineered to take it.
body:
The average time a person spends on any screen before switching to another has collapsed to under a minute. Two decades of careful research confirm what you already feel in your own fractured day, that attention is finite, that it is fragmenting, that constant switching exhausts us and degrades the quality of everything we touch. The distracted feeling is not in your imagination. It is measurable, and it is getting worse, and the device in your hand is the engine of it.

I am not writing this from a clean place. I have looked up from my phone at one in the morning, I have checked it at red lights and during conversations and in the pew, I have felt the strange compulsion to fill every empty second with a glance at the rectangle. This is not a lecture from someone who has it figured out. It is a report from inside the same fight.

## Attention is love

The research frames attention as a productivity asset to be recovered, a resource to be optimized. Scripture frames it as something far weightier. What you behold, you become. What you attend to, you worship. Attention is not a focus technique. It is a form of love, the most basic one, because you cannot love what you will not attend to. To give someone your attention is to give them yourself.

So when your attention is fragmented all day by a device, the loss is not mainly productivity. It is love. You are present to your children with a fraction of yourself because the rest is monitoring a feed. You pray with a divided mind. You cannot sit with God or a friend or your own soul in silence, because the silence has become unbearable and the hand reaches for the phone. Guard your heart, Proverbs says, for it is the wellspring of life. In our day, guarding your heart means guarding your attention, because they have become nearly the same thing.

## You are not weak, you are targeted

The first thing to understand is that this is not a simple failure of willpower, and treating it as one will keep you defeated. The phone is engineered, by thousands of very smart people, to capture and hold your attention, to exploit the exact weaknesses of the human mind. The infinite scroll, the notification, the variable reward that works like a slot machine, all of it is designed. You are not losing this fight because you are weak. You are losing it because you are one tired person against an industry.

This matters because the solution is not mainly more resolve. Resolve loses to design. The solution is to change the design of your own environment, to make the pull harder to obey, because environment beats willpower nearly every time. You will not out-discipline the slot machine. You can put it in another room.

## Make the friction work for you

So the practical moves are mostly about friction. Small repeated actions compound, and changing what sits within arm's reach changes what you do far more reliably than any resolution. The phone within reach gets checked. The phone across the room does not.

Give your phone a bedtime an hour before yours, charging it outside the bedroom, so the day can actually end and the night is not severed by one last scroll. Take one walk with no earbuds, no podcast, no input, and let your mind wander where it will, because the wandering mind is where much of prayer and thought and rest actually happen. Turn off the notifications that are not genuinely urgent, which is almost all of them, because each one is a hand reaching into your attention without your consent. Leave the phone in another room during dinner, during prayer, during the conversation that deserves your whole self. None of this is about resolve. It is about putting the device where the compulsion cannot easily reach it.

## Reclaim the empty seconds

The deepest hook is not the long scroll. It is the empty second. The moment in line, the pause in conversation, the few minutes before sleep, the time that used to be filled with nothing and is now filled with the phone. We have lost our tolerance for empty time, and with it we have lost the places where thought and prayer and noticing used to happen.

Reclaiming those seconds is the real work. The next time you feel the reflex to fill an empty moment, do not fill it. Let it stay empty. Look at the room. Pray a sentence. Notice the person near you. This will feel uncomfortable, even anxious, which tells you how deep the hook goes. Stay with the discomfort. On the other side of it is a mind that can be still, and a self that is present, and a capacity for attention that the device has been quietly eroding.

## This week

Do two small things. Give your phone a bedtime an hour before your own and charge it in another room, three nights at least. And take one walk this week with no earbuds and no destination, letting your mind go wherever it goes. When you catch the reflex to fill an empty second with the screen, just once, do not. Let the second be empty and see what rises into it. You are not trying to defeat the device by sheer will, which will not work. You are taking back your attention one small space at a time, so that you have a self left to give to the people and the God who deserve it.

title: How to Move Your Body as Worship
excerpt: Movement offered as gratitude for a working body is worship. Movement driven by punishment, fear, or the mirror is something else. The difference is everything.
body:
There are two ways to move a body, and they look identical from the outside. Two people run the same three miles, lift the same weights, take the same walk, and one of them is worshiping while the other is punishing. The motion is the same. What drives it is opposite. And because the church has so little to say about the body in motion, most Christians have never been given language to tell the difference, which means many of us are punishing ourselves in the name of health and calling it discipline.

Faithful people land in different places on how much weight bodily training should carry in a Christian life. Some treat regular movement as a stewardship close to essential, since the body is the instrument of every act of service. Others warn that the gym has become a rival sanctuary and commend ordinary unmeasured motion instead, walking, labor, play. Both can be faithful. But both have to watch the same line, and the line is not how much you move. It is why.

## The body is good, so moving it is good

Start with the foundation, because it is easy to forget. The body is good. God made it, called it very good, took one on himself, and intends to raise yours. Movement is one of the plainest ways a body does what it was made to do. To run, to lift, to walk, to dance, to labor with your hands, all of it is a created body being a created body, and there is joy built into it that has nothing to do with results.

Watch a child run for no reason. That is the original meaning of movement, not a means to an end but an expression of being alive in a body that works. Somewhere we lost that and turned movement into a transaction, a way to pay for food or fight off death or fix the reflection. Recovering the joy of motion for its own sake is most of what it means to move as worship.

## The tell is the mirror and the punishment

Here is how you know which kind of movement you are doing. Watch what drives it and how it feels. Movement offered as gratitude for a working body, delight in what it can do, care for the instrument of love, that is stewardship and worship. Movement driven by punishment, by fear of decline, by the reflection that is never lean enough, that is something else, and it should be named gently and brought into the light.

The punishing kind has tells. It is joyless. It is tied to what you ate, a penance for the meal. It is measured obsessively, never enough, always a number to beat or a flaw to fix. It treats the body as an enemy to be subdued rather than a gift to be enjoyed. If your movement is mostly atonement for existing in a body, then exercise has become a false liturgy of self-salvation, and no amount of it will make you feel saved, because that is not what bodies are for.

The worshipful kind is different. It can be enjoyed. It is grateful that the body works at all. It is not chained to the mirror or the scale. It moves because moving is good, the way eating good food is good, received as gift rather than earned as penance.

## A plain word for the wounded

For some readers, movement and the body have become a battleground, tangled up with disordered eating, compulsive exercise, deep shame about appearance. If that is you, this is not a willpower issue to push through, and the answer is not to try harder at the gym. It is a medical and psychological matter that deserves real help, a doctor, a counselor. Please get it. The kind of movement I am describing here, free and grateful, is not available to a body at war with itself, and the war is what needs healing first. There is no shame in needing that help. There is wisdom in seeking it.

## Movement that comes free with a created life

You do not need a gym to move as worship, and for some people the gym is exactly the problem. Much of the best movement comes free with an ordinary embodied life. Walking, with no earbuds and no destination, letting the body and the mind both wander. The labor of a garden, a kitchen, a house. Play with your children. Dancing in the living room. The ordinary motion that humans did for all of history before exercise became a separate scheduled category of penance.

This kind of movement is harder to make into an idol because it cannot be easily measured, and that is its gift. You cannot optimize a walk taken for the joy of walking. You can only take it. Find the motion you can receive as a gift rather than perform as punishment, and do it gently, with nothing tracked and nothing measured, just a body doing what a good body does.

## This week

Move once this week as pure gift, not penance. Take a walk with no earbuds, no tracker, no goal, just the joy of a body that works, and pay attention to how strange it feels to move without measuring it. And if you notice that most of your movement is driven by the mirror or by guilt about food, name that honestly, and if it has become a war, get the help that war needs. You are not paying for your existence with exercise. You are a good body, made by God and bound for resurrection, and you are allowed to move for the simple gladness of moving.

title: How to Receive Rest as a Gift, Not a Reward
excerpt: Most of us only let ourselves rest once the work is done and the rest is earned. But the work is never done, and rest was never a wage. It is a gift, given before you have produced a thing.
body:
Ask most people why they have not rested and the answer comes out the same way. I have not earned it yet. There is too much undone. When I finish, then I will rest. Underneath this is a whole theology, usually unexamined, in which rest is a wage paid out for sufficient productivity, something you have to deserve before you are allowed to have it. And since the work is never actually done, the rest never actually comes, and you spend a life waiting for a permission that will not arrive.

This is exactly backward, and getting it right may change more about your life than any productivity trick ever could. Rest is not a reward you earn at the end of the work. It is a gift given to you as a creature, before you produce anything, woven into the world by a God who rested when there was no exhaustion to recover from.

## God rested before anyone was tired

Go back to the seventh day. God rested, Genesis says, not because he was worn out, since God does not tire, but because rest was built into the design of time as something good in itself. And here is the part we skip. When God made the man, the man's first full day was the seventh, the day of rest. He had not worked yet. His first experience of the world was not labor but Sabbath, rest received before any work was done.

This demolishes the idea that rest is earned. The first human rested before he had produced a single thing, and the rest was no less his for that. Rest is not a wage. It is the air a creature breathes, given freely at the start. We have it exactly upside down when we make it the thing we get only after we have proven ourselves.

## The Sabbath is a declaration of freedom

In Deuteronomy the Sabbath command is grounded in slavery. You were slaves in Egypt, and slaves never get a day off. A slave rests only when the master permits, only when the quota is met, only as a reward for sufficient labor. So your weekly rest is a declaration that you are not a slave anymore, that Pharaoh is not your master, that your worth is no longer measured by your output.

When you refuse to rest until you have earned it, you are living as if Pharaoh were still in charge, as if your value still had to be produced and proven daily. The gift of Sabbath rest is the announcement that this is over, that you are a beloved child and not a unit of production, that you can stop simply because you are allowed to, not because you have earned the right. Every time you rest before the work is done, you preach this to your own anxious heart.

## Receiving is harder than achieving

For a certain kind of person, and I am one, receiving is much harder than achieving. Achieving you control. You put in the effort, you produce the result, you can take credit. Receiving requires you to accept something you did not earn and cannot control, and that is humbling in a way the productive self resists. This is why rest is so hard for the driven. It is not laziness they are avoiding. It is the vulnerability of receiving something for free.

But the gospel is, at its root, the offer of something you cannot earn. Grace is the central word, and grace means a gift given to the undeserving. If you cannot receive the small grace of rest, the gift of a day off you did not earn, you will struggle to receive the large grace of salvation you did not earn either, because they run on the same logic. Learning to rest as a gift is practice for learning to be saved as a gift. The person who can only accept what they have produced cannot finally accept the gospel, which produces nothing and receives everything.

## Rest without apology

The practice, then, is to rest before you feel you deserve it, and to do it without the apology that has become reflex. When you take the day, the walk, the afternoon, the early night, do not narrate to yourself or others all the work that justifies it. Do not earn it in advance and do not pay it off afterward with extra labor. Just receive it, the way you would receive any gift, with thanks rather than a defense.

This will feel wrong at first, even irresponsible. Good. That feeling is the slave-theology protesting, the old conviction that rest must be deserved. Let it protest. Rest anyway. Sleep is the same lesson nightly, a third of your life spent unconscious and unproductive, given to you as a gift by a God who runs the world while you cannot. If you can receive sleep, you can learn to receive rest, and on the far side of that is a freedom most driven people never taste.

## This week

Take one stretch of rest this week that you have not earned, before the work is done, and receive it without apologizing for it. A half day, an afternoon, an early night, with no justification offered and no extra labor paid afterward to make up for it. When the old voice says you have not earned this, answer it plainly, that rest was never a wage and you are not a slave. You are not resting because you finished. You are resting because you are a beloved creature, and the gift was given to you at the start, before you had done a thing.

title: How to Face Your Own Limits Without Despair
excerpt: You are a creature, and creatures come with edges. The need to sleep, to rest, to stop, is not a design flaw to engineer around. It is a built-in rehearsal of humility, and a gift.
body:
There is a particular kind of suffering that comes from refusing to be finite. You have more to do than there are hours. You need more sleep than you allow yourself. You want to be present in more places than one body can occupy, to help more people than you have capacity for, to hold up more than your two hands can carry. And underneath the exhaustion is a quiet, exhausting belief, that the limit itself is the enemy, that if you were just disciplined enough or efficient enough you could finally outrun your own edges. You cannot. The edges are not a problem to solve. They are the truth of what you are.

This is one of the deepest spiritual issues in the body, and the church rarely names it. We treat our limits as failures, as things to apologize for and push past, when in fact the limits are the gift, the built-in correction to the oldest lie, that we could be like God. Facing your limits without despair is most of what it means to be at peace in a body.

## The limit is built in, and it is good

You need to spend a third of your life unconscious. That is not a design flaw to be engineered around. It is a nightly rehearsal of humility, an enforced admission that the world runs without you for eight hours at a stretch and is fine in the morning. The people who resent sleep most are usually the ones most convinced the world cannot run without them, and sleep is God's nightly contradiction of that conviction.

Sabbath says weekly what sleep says nightly. The world was running before you woke and it will keep running after you stop, and the God who holds it does not get tired. The limit is not a punishment. It is a mercy, a regular reminder that you are not the one holding everything together, which is a crushing job you were never given and cannot do. Every edge you bump against, the need to sleep, to eat, to stop, to say no, is the gentle insistence of your own creatureliness, and creatureliness is good. God made it and called it very good.

## Despair comes from believing the limit is failure

The despair sets in when you mistake the limit for a moral failing. You cannot do it all, so you conclude you are not enough. You need rest, so you feel weak. You have to disappoint someone because you cannot be everywhere, and you carry it as guilt. This is the despair of a creature trying to be God and grieving that it cannot. The cure is not to try harder. It is to repent of the ambition that you should have no limits in the first place.

The truth that sets you free is that your limits were never yours to overcome. They are the shape of how you were made. You were not designed to be infinite, and the fact that you are not is not a defect. The despair lifts when you stop measuring yourself against a standard meant for God alone and start receiving the freedom of being a creature, who is allowed to be finite, allowed to need rest, allowed to do what one person can do and trust God with the rest.

## Your limits are an act of faith in someone else

Here is the turn that changes everything. When you accept a limit, you are not just admitting your own smallness. You are confessing your faith that someone larger is at work. You stop because you trust that God does not. You sleep because you trust he keeps the watch. You say no to one good thing because you trust that your refusal does not unravel the world, that the need you cannot meet is held by a God who can.

This is why the refusal to accept limits is, at bottom, a failure of faith dressed as diligence. The person who cannot stop, cannot rest, cannot say no, is functionally claiming that it all depends on them, that if they let go for a moment everything falls. Accepting your limits is the practical, embodied confession that it does not all depend on you, that there is a God, and you are not him, and that is unspeakably good news.

## When the limits are heavier

For some, the limit is not just the ordinary finitude of a healthy body but the harder limits of illness, disability, chronic pain, aging, a body that can do far less than it once could. I do not want to wave these away with cheerful words. They are heavier, and the grief is real. If you are facing limits like these, get the real help they require, medical and otherwise, and let yourself mourn what has been taken. But even here, the deepest word holds. Your worth was never your capacity. Paul learned that God's power is made perfect in weakness, that the limit itself can become the place where grace shows up most clearly. The body that can do less is not worth less. It is held by the same hands.

## Number your days

The final limit is death, and a Christian can look even at that without despair. Teach us to number our days, the psalmist prays, that we may get a heart of wisdom. Numbering your days means accepting that you have a finite number of them, that you are not infinite in time any more than in strength, and that wisdom comes precisely from making peace with that. This body will weaken, fail, and be laid down. And then, by the mercy of God, be raised. The last limit is not the end. It is the door.

## This week

Find one limit you have been fighting and accept it on purpose this week. Say no to one good thing you do not have capacity for, and do not apologize for it. Go to bed before the work is done, as a confession that the world holds together without you. When the despair whispers that your limit means you are not enough, answer it with the truth, that you were never meant to be infinite, that the edges are a gift, and that there is a God who holds what you cannot. You are a creature. That is not your failure. It is the good thing you were made to be.
